title: I Love You and I'm Proud of You, What Dean L. Stuart Taught Me About Teaching
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart uses his late grandfather's ritual farewell, I love you and I'm proud of you, as a frame for what teachers owe students. The phrase, he says, teaches that correction and affection coexist, so teachers must remain in each student's corner even after hard conversations. It also teaches presence, achieved through small systems such as remembering birthdays and not trading planning time for venting. The pride half of the phrase leads to his claim that teachers should work at becoming respectable people instead of engineering student respect. He ends with a poignant reflection that a single teacher might have changed the course of a life, which is why teaching is noble work.
points: Hard conversations should end by reaffirming that the teacher is still for the student, the foundation of management and relationships.
Presence for dozens of students is achieved through simple systems, not heroic attendance at every event.
Teaching from love means treating students as you would want your own children treated.
Earned respect comes from becoming a more respectable person through disciplined habits, not from tactics.
Even small interventions by teachers can alter a young person's trajectory, which gives the work its weight.
quotes: But Grandpa ended the difficult conversations with the same, “I love you and I’m proud of you.” In doing this, he affirmed that even when we messed up, he was for us.

Effective classroom management and quality student-teacher relationships are built on the same idea: yesterday, Calvin may have done something disrespectful; after I address the issue with Calvin, I need reaffirm, to him and to myself, that I am still his teacher, still in his corner.
Perfection isn't possible, but consistent effort toward being for our kids is.

We can be present for our students when we decide to come up with simple systems for remembering kids’ birthdays. We can be present when we stop trading planning time for time spent complaining or venting about kids.

Nine years into the work, I’ve come to see it’s frustrating and only moderately effective to try to engineer student respect; it’s much more efficient and beneficial, for everyone in our lives, if we instead work at becoming someone respectable.
I can’t help but think that a teacher — just one teacher — could have saved his life.
That kind of potential is in every day that we work with students. That’s why this is a noble profession, and why it’s hard, and why it’s good.
